title: Yepun and the Milky Way
caption: Yepun, the VLT's fourth Unit Telescope, under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Lit by the stars of the Milky Way, a large telescope enclosure stands on the summit of Cerro Paranal, poised for a night of observing. This is Yepun, the fourth Unit Telescope (UT4) of ESO's Very Large Telescope, photographed by John Colosimo.

Yepun carries a main mirror 8.2 meters across and is one of four Unit Telescopes that make up the VLT. Its companions are Antu, Kueyen and Melipal. The four names come from the language of the Mapuche people and mean, in turn, Venus, the Sun, the Moon and the Southern Cross. Combined, the four telescopes act as the VLT Interferometer, which lets astronomers pick out details up to 16 times finer than a single telescope can.

Near the plane of the Milky Way, at the heart of Scorpius, shines the red star Antares. Around it the stars are so crowded that most other objects and constellations are hard to make out. The shutter stayed open for 30 seconds, long enough for Earth's rotation to stretch each star into a short trail.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph of the observatory taken by John Colosimo with a 30-second exposure. The source does not publish camera or color-processing details.
understand.eye: Over those seconds the camera gathered far more light than an eye takes in at once, and Earth's rotation turned the stars into short trails where a naked-eye observer would see points.

explore: Paranal Observatory sits 2635 meters above sea level and is ESO's flagship facility, which ESO calls the most advanced ground-based astronomical observatory in the world. The Mapuche people, whose language gave the telescopes their names, have their homeland some 500 kilometers to the south of Santiago de Chile. Antares ranks as the sixteenth brightest star in the night sky.
alt: A large telescope enclosure on a mountaintop under a star-filled Milky Way, with the red star Antares visible and stars drawn into short trails.
